IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p230/r1.claim: A man from Banu Salama blamed Kaʿb's clothes and vanity for his absence; Muʿadh rebuked him and testified that he knew only good of Kaʿb, while the Prophet stayed silent.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p230/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p230/r2.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p230/r2.claim: More than eighty absentees offered excuses and oaths; the Prophet accepted their outward professions, sought forgiveness for them, and left their inner realities to God.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p230/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p230/r3.speaker: كعب بن مالك
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p230/r3.claim: On hearing the Prophet was returning, Kaʿb considered lies but concluded he could not escape God's knowledge and resolved to tell the truth.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p230/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p230/r4.speaker: كعب بن مالك
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p230/r4.claim: Kaʿb admits he had no excuse and was fully able to go; the Prophet confirms his truthfulness and tells him to wait for God's judgment.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p230/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p230/r5.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p230/r5.claim: After Kaʿb tells the truth, the Prophet says he has spoken truly and orders him to wait until God decides his case.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p230/r6.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p230/r6.speaker: كعب بن مالك
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p230/r6.claim: Some Banu Salama urged Kaʿb to make an excuse like the others; he nearly recanted, then learned that Murara and Hilal had also told the truth.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p231#2/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p231#2/r1.speaker: كعب بن مالك
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p231#2/r1.claim: Kaʿb refused to seek permission to keep his wife, unsure what a young man would be told; after ten more nights, the three completed fifty nights of silence.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p231#2/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p231#2/r2.speaker: كعب بن مالك
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p231#2/r2.claim: On the fiftieth morning, while Kaʿb felt the earth and his soul constrict, a caller on Mount Sala announced good news; he prostrated, recognizing that relief had come.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p231#2/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p231#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p231#2/r3.claim: News of God's acceptance reached the Prophet at dawn; messengers hurried to the three, and the caller's voice outran a mounted messenger.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p231#2/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p231#2/r4.speaker: كعب بن مالك
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p231#2/r4.claim: Kaʿb gave the two garments he owned to the man who brought the news, then borrowed two garments and set out for the Messenger.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p231#2/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p231#2/r5.speaker: كعب بن مالك
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p231#2/r5.claim: Talha alone among the Emigrants stood to congratulate Kaʿb, who never forgot it; the joyful Prophet called this the best day since Kaʿb's birth and said the good news came from God.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p231#2/r6.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p231#2/r6.speaker: كعب بن مالك
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p231#2/r6.claim: Kaʿb offered to give all his wealth in charity, but the Prophet told him to retain some, so he kept his share at Khaybar; Kaʿb vowed to speak only truth thereafter.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p231#2/r7.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p231#2/r7.speaker: كعب بن مالك
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p231#2/r7.claim: Kaʿb regards his truthful confession as his greatest blessing after Islam and hopes God will preserve his truthfulness for life.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p231#2/r8.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p231#2/r8.speaker: كعب بن مالك
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p231#2/r8.claim: God revealed the account of the three and the command to be with the truthful; Kaʿb contrasts their truthful confession with those who lied and were condemned.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p231#2/r9.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p231#2/r9.speaker: كعب بن مالك
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p231#2/r9.claim: The Prophet accepted the oath-taking absentees and sought forgiveness for them but postponed the three truthful men's case; khalafu here means deferred, not merely staying behind from battle.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p231/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p231/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p231/r1.claim: The Prophet prohibited Muslims from speaking to the three truthful absentees; the boycott lasted fifty nights, making even familiar earth seem strange to Kaʿb.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p231/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p231/r2.speaker: كعب بن مالك
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p231/r2.claim: Murara and Hilal stayed home crying, while Kaʿb kept attending prayer and markets; people ignored him, and the Prophet looked away when Kaʿb sought his gaze.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p231/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p231/r3.speaker: كعب بن مالك
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p231/r3.claim: Kaʿb asked his cousin Abu Qatada to affirm his love for God and the Messenger; Abu Qatada stayed silent, then replied that God and His Messenger knew best, and Kaʿb wept.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p231/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p231/r4.speaker: كعب بن مالك
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p231/r4.claim: A Ghassan ruler's letter said the Prophet had abandoned Kaʿb and invited him to join; Kaʿb recognized this as another trial and burned it.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p231/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p231/r5.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p231/r5.claim: After forty nights the Prophet ordered the three to separate from their wives; Hilal's wife was allowed to serve her helpless, grieving elderly husband but not approach him.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p233/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p233/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p233/r1.claim: The account of the three is sound and agreed upon by Bukhari and Muslim; Ibn Kathir says it gives the verse's clearest and fullest interpretation.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p233/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p233/r2.speaker: جابر بن عبد الله
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p233/r2.claim: Jabir identifies the three as Kaʿb ibn Malik, Hilal ibn Umayya, and Murara ibn Rabiʿa, all from the Ansar.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p233/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p233/r3.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p233/r3.claim: Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Qatada, al-Suddi, and others identify Murara; reports vary between forms of his name, but Ibn Kathir prefers Murara ibn al-Rabiʿa, matching the two Sahih collections.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p233/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p233/r4.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p233/r4.claim: The report that two of the three had fought at Badr is probably a mistake by al-Zuhri, since none of the three is known to have attended Badr.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p233/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p233/r5.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p233/r5.claim: Muslim estrangement closed every route for the three for nearly fifty days; they endured patiently and were finally relieved because they truthfully admitted having no excuse.

BIQAI-FULL:v3p397/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v3p397/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v3p397/r1.claim: After mentioning repentance for those near to deviation alongside the steadfast, the passage turns to those who did deviate without naming their fault, preserving their dignity and consoling them.

BIQAI-FULL:v3p397/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v3p397/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v3p397/r2.claim: The opening phrase means that God had indeed turned toward and forgiven the three who had been left behind.

BIQAI-FULL:v3p397/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v3p397/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v3p397/r3.claim: They were left behind through the Messenger's boycott, as he and the people stopped speaking to them while their judgment awaited God's decision.

BIQAI-FULL:v3p397/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v3p397/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v3p397/r4.claim: The earth's being constricted despite its spaciousness uses an elevated expression to stress the severity: everywhere felt narrow to them.

BIQAI-FULL:v3p398/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v3p398/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v3p398/r1.claim: Their failure was severe because they disobeyed the Messenger, withheld companionship, preferred themselves, and committed other grave offenses.

BIQAI-FULL:v3p398/r11.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v3p398/r11.speaker: كعب
BIQAI-FULL:v3p398/r11.claim: Al-Biqai notes that al-Bukhari records Ka'b's account of the repentance of one of the three in several places in his Sahih.

BIQAI-FULL:v3p398/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v3p398/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v3p398/r2.claim: He says fear of God's majesty can be grounded on the conviction that no cause leads to Him except through Him, since He encompasses all things.

BIQAI-FULL:v3p398/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v3p398/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v3p398/r3.claim: He suggests ثم marks the length of their ordeal and fear, and God's favor in eventually returning them.

BIQAI-FULL:v3p398/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v3p398/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v3p398/r4.claim: The delay in judgment singled them out because of their high prior standing as leaders; even a slight lapse by guides is weighty.

BIQAI-FULL:v3p398/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v3p398/r5.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v3p398/r5.claim: Despite the grave disobedience of leaving the Messenger and failing to support him, God's second repentance purified them and raised them toward greater knowledge and closeness.

BIQAI-FULL:v3p398/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v3p398/r6.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v3p398/r6.claim: The first repentance enables them to return to their original sound disposition, steadfastness, religious excellence, and the character of the earliest believers.

BIQAI-FULL:v3p398/r7.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v3p398/r7.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v3p398/r7.claim: He suggests ثم may signal the length of their ordeal and God's favor; their high prior rank explains the delayed ruling, since a small lapse by leaders is more serious than much by others.

BIQAI-FULL:v3p398/r8.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v3p398/r8.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v3p398/r8.claim: Al-Tawwab emphasizes that God accepts repentance even after grave and repeated sins; al-Rahim emphasizes His preserving and abundantly favoring the servants He wills.

DURR-FULL:v4p276/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p276/r1.speaker: الضحاك
DURR-FULL:v4p276/r1.claim: The phrase about God turning to them is glossed as their setting things right, linking divine acceptance with their repentance.

DURR-FULL:v4p276/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p276/r4.speaker: سعيد بن المسيب
DURR-FULL:v4p276/r4.claim: After returning from Tabuk, Abu Lubaba was shunned, bound himself to a pillar for seven days without food or water, and remained until God announced his repentance.

DURR-FULL:v4p277/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p277/r1.speaker: author
DURR-FULL:v4p277/r1.claim: Some people thought the stragglers were doomed because no excuse had been granted, while others hoped for repentance; they remained deferred until verses 9:117–118 announced it.

DURR-FULL:v4p278/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p278/r3.speaker: جابر بن عبد الله
DURR-FULL:v4p278/r3.claim: Ka'b, Murara, and Hilal were deferred for forty days, isolated from their wives and the Muslims; after verse 9:118 descended, Umm Salama sent Ka'b the good news.

DURR-FULL:v4p278/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p278/r6.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
DURR-FULL:v4p278/r6.claim: In a vision, the Prophet saw a man whose head was repeatedly crushed by a rock and restored before being struck again.

DURR-FULL:v4p309/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p309/r3.speaker: جابر بن عبد الله
DURR-FULL:v4p309/r3.claim: Jabir identifies the three left behind as Ka'b ibn Malik, Hilal ibn Umayya, and Murara ibn al-Rabi', all Ansar.

DURR-FULL:v4p309/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p309/r4.speaker: مجمع بن جارية
DURR-FULL:v4p309/r4.claim: He identifies the three whose repentance God accepted as Ka'b, Hilal, and Murara.

DURR-FULL:v4p309/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p309/r5.speaker: ابن شهاب
DURR-FULL:v4p309/r5.claim: Ibn Shihab identifies the three and gives their tribal affiliations: Ka'b of Banu Salima, Hilal of Banu Waqif, and Murara of Banu Amr ibn Awf.

DURR-FULL:v4p309/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p309/r6.speaker: أنس بن مالك
DURR-FULL:v4p309/r6.claim: On return from Tabuk, the Prophet ordered companions not to speak or sit with those who stayed behind; he later accepted their pledge and prayed for forgiveness, while naming three sincere stragglers without hypocrisy.

DURR-FULL:v4p309/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p309/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v4p309/r7.claim: Ibn Abbas gives the same three names: Ka'b, Murara, and Hilal.

DURR-FULL:v4p309/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p309/r8.speaker: كعب بن مالك
DURR-FULL:v4p309/r8.claim: Ka'b says he never missed a campaign except Tabuk and Badr; no one was blamed for missing Badr because the Prophet had set out for the Quraysh caravan and met the enemy unexpectedly, while the Aqaba pledge mattered more to him than famous Badr.

DURR-FULL:v4p313#2/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p313#2/r1.speaker: كعب بن مالك
DURR-FULL:v4p313#2/r1.claim: Ka'b pledged to speak only truth, says he had not knowingly lied since, and regards telling the truth to the Prophet as his greatest blessing because the liars were condemned.

DURR-FULL:v4p313#2/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p313#2/r2.speaker: كعب بن مالك
DURR-FULL:v4p313#2/r2.claim: He distinguishes his group from those whose excuses the Prophet accepted: the other men swore excuses, were accepted, pledged, and received prayers for forgiveness; the three's case was deferred until God's judgment.

DURR-FULL:v4p313#2/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p313#2/r3.speaker: كعب بن مالك
DURR-FULL:v4p313#2/r3.claim: Ka'b clarifies that the verse's wording about being left behind refers to the Prophet deferring their case, not merely their failure to join the expedition.

DURR-FULL:v4p313#2/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p313#2/r4.speaker: كعب بن مالك
DURR-FULL:v4p313#2/r4.claim: When his repentance was announced, Ka'b kissed the Prophet's hand and knee and gave the bearer of the news two garments.

DURR-FULL:v4p313#2/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p313#2/r5.speaker: مجاهد
DURR-FULL:v4p313#2/r5.claim: The three are those whose case was deferred in the middle of Surat Bara'a: Hilal, Murara, and Ka'b.

DURR-FULL:v4p313#2/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p313#2/r6.speaker: قتادة
DURR-FULL:v4p313#2/r6.claim: He explains the strengthened reading of “left behind” as being held back from the Tabuk expedition.

DURR-FULL:v4p314/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p314/r1.speaker: الحسن
DURR-FULL:v4p314/r1.claim: Hasan recounts three different regrets: one left to enjoy a fruitful orchard then gave it in charity, another stayed with his reunited family and vowed not to return until God's judgment, and a third pursued the army over rough ground until he caught up.

DURR-FULL:v4p314/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p314/r2.speaker: الحسن
DURR-FULL:v4p314/r2.claim: Hasan stresses that the three took no unlawful wealth or blood and caused no corruption; their fault was delaying a degree of jihad, yet the sin weighed heavily on believers.

DURR-FULL:v4p314/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p314/r3.speaker: الضحاك
DURR-FULL:v4p314/r3.claim: Al-Dahhak says the three were left waiting for repentance until God accepted Abu Lubaba and his companions.

DURR-FULL:v4p314/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p314/r4.speaker: عكرمة
DURR-FULL:v4p314/r4.claim: Ikrima likewise glosses “left behind” as being deferred from repentance.

DURR-FULL:v4p315/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p315/r1.speaker: عكرمة بن خالد المخزومي
DURR-FULL:v4p315/r1.claim: Ikrima ibn Khalid al-Makhzumi recites the phrase with the three in the accusative and explains it as after Muhammad and his companions.

DURR-FULL:v4p315/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p315/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v4p315/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas says God invited even Pharaoh to repentance; no one may make people despair of it, and repentance begins with God's enabling turn toward the servant.

BURSEVI:v3p398#2/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v3p398#2/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v3p398#2/r1.claim: ‘The three left behind’ are those whose case was deferred without a ruling until revelation: Kaʿb ibn Mālik, Murāra ibn al-Rabīʿ, and Hilāl ibn Umayya.

BURSEVI:v3p398#2/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v3p398#2/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v3p398#2/r2.claim: The earth became narrow when people avoided speaking or even greeting them; they feared dying without the Prophet or believers praying over them.

BURSEVI:v3p398#2/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v3p398#2/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v3p398#2/r3.claim: Their souls were so filled with loneliness that no room remained for comfort or joy; saying these were constricted ‘upon them’ stresses their utter distress.

BURSEVI:v3p398#3/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v3p398#3/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v3p398#3/r1.claim: They knew there was no refuge from God's anger except turning to Him for forgiveness; ‘they thought’ means ‘they knew,’ since this is praise and praise requires knowledge.

BURSEVI:v3p398#3/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v3p398#3/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v3p398#3/r2.claim: Grammatically, an omitted pronoun of ‘the matter’ is the subject of softened anna; the clause fills both objects of ‘they thought,’ with exception from an omitted general term.

BURSEVI:v3p398#3/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v3p398#3/r3.speaker: بعض المتقدمين
BURSEVI:v3p398#3/r3.claim: An early saying advises frequent gratitude when blessings accumulate and frequent seeking forgiveness when worries multiply.

BURSEVI:v3p398#3/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v3p398#3/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v3p398#3/r4.claim: One immersed in divine unity sees only God in existence and seeks refuge only in Him; visible forms and places are merely causes.

BURSEVI:v3p398#3/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v3p398#3/r5.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v3p398#3/r5.claim: Rūmī's Mathnawī compares a visible form to a shadow and urges seeking the reflected person, turning from secondary causes to the ultimate Causer.

BURSEVI:v3p399/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v3p399/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v3p399/r1.claim: ‘Then He turned to them’ means He enabled them to repent; ‘so they might repent’ means they returned from sin.

BURSEVI:v3p399/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v3p399/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v3p399/r2.claim: He distinguishes God's enabling, the person's repentance, and God's acceptance; enabling precedes acceptance by two ranks, so thumma signals rank rather than time.

BURSEVI:v3p399/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v3p399/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v3p399/r3.claim: Alternatively, ‘He turned to them’ means He announced acceptance and ‘so they might repent’ means they became counted among the repentant; thumma then keeps its ordinary temporal sense.

BURSEVI:v3p399/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v3p399/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v3p399/r4.claim: God is repeatedly accepting and merciful, accepting a repentant person even after a hundred returns while favoring people who deserve punishment.

BURSEVI:v3p399/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v3p399/r5.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v3p399/r5.claim: A Persian couplet says repentance needs hope of acceptance and a broken or uncertain vow does not complete sincere repentance.

BURSEVI:v3p399/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v3p399/r6.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v3p399/r6.claim: Some believers who had lagged behind regretted it and caught up with the Prophet.

BURSEVI:v3p399/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v3p399/r7.speaker: الحسن
BURSEVI:v3p399/r7.claim: Al-Ḥasan recounts three cases: one leaves a valuable orchard that held him back, another his family, and a third his love of life; each crosses hardship to rejoin the Prophet.

BURSEVI:v3p399/r8.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v3p399/r8.speaker: أبو ذر الغفاري
BURSEVI:v3p399/r8.claim: Abū Dharr's camel delayed him, so he carried his belongings on his back and followed the Prophet on foot.

ALUSI-FULL:v11p41/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v11p41/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v11p41/r1.claim: The phrase 'and the three' is coordinated with the mention of the Prophet and shares the verb 'turned'; inserting an implicit 'turned' has been proposed because their repentance differs, but the author finds that unnecessary.

ALUSI-FULL:v11p41/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v11p41/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v11p41/r2.claim: The three were left behind in judgment and their case postponed: no excuse was accepted or rejected until revelation came; the wording may be figurative or imply their case, or it may mean that they themselves stayed behind from the campaign.

ALUSI-FULL:v11p41/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v11p41/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v11p41/r3.claim: They were Kaʿb b. Malik, Hilal b. Umayya, and Murara b. al-Rabiʿ; Muslim and others call Murara al-Amiri, while many hadith scholars correct this to al-Umari.

ALUSI-FULL:v11p41/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v11p41/r4.speaker: عكرمة
ALUSI-FULL:v11p41/r4.claim: Ikrima, Ruzayn b. Hubaysh, and ʿAmr b. ʿUbayd read خلفوا with light lām and explain it as being left behind in Medina or becoming corrupt; ʿAli b. al-Husayn, al-Baqir, Jaʿfar al-Sadiq, and al-Sulami read خالفوا, while al-Aʿmash reads المخلفين.

ALUSI-FULL:v11p41/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v11p41/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v11p41/r5.claim: The earth's constriction marks the end of their delayed case: people shunned them under the Prophet's order, and the image means they could not settle in the world despite its breadth; a cited poetic line evokes the fear of the pursued.

ALUSI-FULL:v11p41/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v11p41/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v11p41/r6.claim: Their selves are their hearts; the heart's constriction means grief with no room for joy, and the move from constricted earth to constricted selves heightens the rhetoric.

ALUSI-FULL:v11p41/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v11p41/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v11p41/r7.claim: They knew there was no refuge from God's displeasure except seeking His forgiveness and repenting to Him; ظنوا here means they knew.

ALUSI-FULL:v11p41/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v11p41/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v11p41/r8.claim: God's turning to them may mean enabling them to repent, revealing their acceptance in the Qur'an, or repeatedly returning with mercy so they persist in repentance; another view says He accepted their lapse so that they could repent again without despair.

ALUSI-FULL:v11p41/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v11p41/r9.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v11p41/r9.claim: God is repeatedly accepting repentance, even if a person returns to sin a hundred times in one day, and mercifully grants blessings despite their deserving punishment.

ALUSI-FULL:v11p42#2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v11p42#2/r1.speaker: معاذ بن جبل
ALUSI-FULL:v11p42#2/r1.claim: A man of Banu Salama blamed Kaʿb's absence on vanity and fine clothes; Muʿadh rebuked him and testified that he knew only good of Kaʿb.

ALUSI-FULL:v11p42#2/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v11p42#2/r2.speaker: كعب بن مالك
ALUSI-FULL:v11p42#2/r2.claim: When he heard the Prophet was returning, Kaʿb considered inventing an excuse but recognized that lying could not save him and resolved to tell the truth.

ALUSI-FULL:v11p42#2/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v11p42#2/r3.speaker: كعب بن مالك
ALUSI-FULL:v11p42#2/r3.claim: About eighty men offered excuses; the Prophet accepted their outward professions, sought forgiveness for them, and left their hidden intentions to God.

ALUSI-FULL:v11p42#2/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v11p42#2/r4.speaker: كعب بن مالك
ALUSI-FULL:v11p42#2/r4.claim: Kaʿb confessed that he had no excuse and had been able to go; the Prophet affirmed his truthfulness and deferred judgment to God.

ALUSI-FULL:v11p42#2/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v11p42#2/r5.speaker: كعب بن مالك
ALUSI-FULL:v11p42#2/r5.claim: Two other truthful veterans of Badr, Marārah ibn al-Rabīʿ and Hilāl ibn Umayya, gave the same answer and shared Kaʿb's fate.

ALUSI-FULL:v11p42#2/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v11p42#2/r6.speaker: كعب بن مالك
ALUSI-FULL:v11p42#2/r6.claim: The Prophet prohibited people from speaking to the three, and the estrangement lasted fifty nights, making the familiar earth feel alien to Kaʿb.

ALUSI-FULL:v11p42#2/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v11p42#2/r7.speaker: كعب بن مالك
ALUSI-FULL:v11p42#2/r7.claim: During the boycott Kaʿb still attended prayer and walked the markets, but nobody spoke to him; he watched for a response from the Prophet.

ALUSI-FULL:v11p42#2/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v11p42#2/r8.speaker: كعب بن مالك
ALUSI-FULL:v11p42#2/r8.claim: The Prophet would turn toward Kaʿb while he prayed but turn away when Kaʿb looked at him.

ALUSI-FULL:v11p42/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v11p42/r1.speaker: كعب بن مالك
ALUSI-FULL:v11p42/r1.claim: Kaʿb's account says he missed no campaign except Tabuk, though he had missed Badr without blame because the Prophet had set out for the Quraysh caravan and met the enemy unexpectedly; Kaʿb valued the Aqaba pledge above Badr despite Badr's greater fame.

ALUSI-FULL:v11p42/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v11p42/r2.speaker: كعب بن مالك
ALUSI-FULL:v11p42/r2.claim: Kaʿb says that before Tabuk he had never been stronger or wealthier and had never owned two mounts for a campaign; the Prophet announced the destination because the journey was long and difficult, the weather hot, and the enemy numerous.

ALUSI-FULL:v11p42/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v11p42/r3.speaker: كعب بن مالك
ALUSI-FULL:v11p42/r3.claim: The Muslim force was so large it had no single register; a would-be deserter thought his absence might remain unknown without revelation, and the expedition began when fruit and shade were appealing.

ALUSI-FULL:v11p42/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v11p42/r4.speaker: كعب بن مالك
ALUSI-FULL:v11p42/r4.claim: Kaʿb repeatedly went out intending to prepare, returned having done nothing, and delayed until the army departed; although he considered catching up, he never did, and later saw only suspected hypocrites or people excused by God among those left behind.

ALUSI-FULL:v11p42/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v11p42/r5.speaker: كعب بن مالك
ALUSI-FULL:v11p42/r5.claim: At Tabuk, while seated among his companions, the Prophet asked what had happened to Kaʿb b. Malik.

ALUSI-FULL:v11p43/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v11p43/r1.speaker: كعب بن مالك
ALUSI-FULL:v11p43/r1.claim: Kaʿb repeatedly asked his cousin Abū Qatāda whether he knew Kaʿb loved God and His Messenger; Abū Qatāda replied that God and His Messenger knew best, and Kaʿb wept.

ALUSI-FULL:v11p43/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v11p43/r2.speaker: كعب بن مالك
ALUSI-FULL:v11p43/r2.claim: A letter from the Ghassānī ruler invited Kaʿb to join him because the Prophet had supposedly cast him aside; Kaʿb treated the offer as another trial and burned it.

ALUSI-FULL:v11p43/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v11p43/r3.speaker: رسول الله
ALUSI-FULL:v11p43/r3.claim: After forty days of the boycott, a messenger ordered Kaʿb and the other two to separate from their wives, clarifying that they need not divorce them but must not approach them.

ALUSI-FULL:v11p43/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v11p43/r4.speaker: رسول الله
ALUSI-FULL:v11p43/r4.claim: The Prophet allowed Hilāl's elderly wife, who had no helper, to serve him, but forbade marital intimacy; she said Hilāl had wept continually.

ALUSI-FULL:v11p43/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v11p43/r5.speaker: كعب بن مالك
ALUSI-FULL:v11p43/r5.claim: Kaʿb sent his wife to her family and refused to seek permission to keep her, uncertain how the Prophet would answer and mindful that he was young.

ALUSI-FULL:v11p43/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v11p43/r6.speaker: كعب بن مالك
ALUSI-FULL:v11p43/r6.claim: At dawn after the fiftieth night, while sitting in the distress described by the verse, Kaʿb heard a caller on Mount Sal announce God's acceptance of their repentance and prostrated.

ALUSI-FULL:v11p43/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v11p43/r7.speaker: كعب بن مالك
ALUSI-FULL:v11p43/r7.claim: People hurried to bring the news, and the caller's voice reached Kaʿb before the mounted messenger; Kaʿb gave the messenger the only two garments he owned and borrowed replacements.

ALUSI-FULL:v11p44/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v11p44/r1.speaker: كعب بن مالك
ALUSI-FULL:v11p44/r1.claim: Ṭalḥa ibn ʿUbayd Allāh alone among the Emigrants rose, hurried to greet Kaʿb, and congratulated him; Kaʿb never forgot this kindness.

ALUSI-FULL:v11p44/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v11p44/r2.speaker: رسول الله
ALUSI-FULL:v11p44/r2.claim: The Prophet told Kaʿb this was the best day of his life since his mother bore him, and clarified that the good news came from God.

ALUSI-FULL:v11p44/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v11p44/r3.speaker: كعب بن مالك
ALUSI-FULL:v11p44/r3.claim: Kaʿb offered to give all his wealth in charity as repentance, but the Prophet advised him to keep some; he retained his share at Khaybar.

ALUSI-FULL:v11p44/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v11p44/r4.speaker: كعب بن مالك
ALUSI-FULL:v11p44/r4.claim: Kaʿb resolved to speak only truth for the rest of his life, credited truthful confession with his salvation, and said he had not deliberately lied since making that vow.

ALUSI-FULL:v11p44/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v11p44/r5.speaker: كعب بن مالك
ALUSI-FULL:v11p44/r5.claim: Kaʿb says the verse of their repentance was revealed and regards his truthful answer as a greater blessing than anything received after Islam, unlike those who lied.

ALUSI-FULL:v11p44/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v11p44/r6.speaker: كعب بن مالك
ALUSI-FULL:v11p44/r6.claim: In another account Kaʿb feared dying ostracized or outliving the Prophet in permanent isolation; Umm Salama advocated for him, and the Prophet announced their pardon after dawn prayer to spare them a sleepless crowd.

ALUSI-FULL:v11p44/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v11p44/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v11p44/r7.claim: The description of the three's distress demonstrates the strength of their faith and the sincerity of their repentance.

ALUSI-FULL:v11p44/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v11p44/r8.speaker: أبو بكر الوراق
ALUSI-FULL:v11p44/r8.claim: Al-Warrāq defines sincere repentance through the constriction of the repentant person's world and soul, exemplified by Kaʿb and his two companions.

ELMALILI:9:118#2/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:9:118#2/r1.speaker: Ka‘b b. Mâlik
ELMALILI:9:118#2/r1.claim: Ka‘b says he missed no expedition besides Tabūk except Badr, for which the Prophet did not reproach anyone; he valued his pledge at al-‘Aqaba above having fought at Badr.

ELMALILI:9:118#2/r10.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:9:118#2/r10.speaker: Ka‘b b. Mâlik
ELMALILI:9:118#2/r10.claim: The Prophet affirmed that Ka‘b had spoken truthfully and ordered him to rise and wait until God judged his case.

ELMALILI:9:118#2/r11.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:9:118#2/r11.speaker: Ka‘b b. Mâlik
ELMALILI:9:118#2/r11.claim: Some Banū Salima men urged Ka‘b to give an excuse like the others, saying the Prophet’s prayer would suffice; he nearly retracted, but learned Murāra and Hilāl had also told the truth and stayed firm.

ELMALILI:9:118#2/r12.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:9:118#2/r12.speaker: Ka‘b b. Mâlik
ELMALILI:9:118#2/r12.claim: The Prophet forbade Muslims to speak with the three, and people shunned them for fifty nights; Ka‘b’s familiar land became strange, while his two companions stayed home weeping.

ELMALILI:9:118#2/r13.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:9:118#2/r13.speaker: Ka‘b b. Mâlik
ELMALILI:9:118#2/r13.claim: Ka‘b continued attending communal prayers and greeting the Prophet, but the Prophet turned away when their eyes met; Ka‘b’s cousin Abū Qatāda also initially refused to answer whether he knew Ka‘b loved God and His Messenger.

ELMALILI:9:118#2/r14.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:9:118#2/r14.speaker: Ka‘b b. Mâlik
ELMALILI:9:118#2/r14.claim: A man from Syria brought Ka‘b a letter from the king of Ghassān offering refuge and support; Ka‘b called it another trial and burned it.

ELMALILI:9:118#2/r15.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:9:118#2/r15.speaker: Ka‘b b. Mâlik
ELMALILI:9:118#2/r15.claim: After forty nights, the Prophet ordered the three to separate from their wives, not divorce them. Hilāl’s wife received permission to serve her elderly, helpless husband without approaching him; Ka‘b declined to ask for similar permission because he was young.

ELMALILI:9:118#2/r16.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:9:118#2/r16.speaker: Ka‘b b. Mâlik
ELMALILI:9:118#2/r16.claim: On the fiftieth morning, while deeply constricted as the verse describes, Ka‘b heard news on Mount Sal‘ that God had accepted their repentance; he prostrated, and messengers hurried to tell the companions.

ELMALILI:9:118#2/r17.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:9:118#2/r17.speaker: Ka‘b b. Mâlik
ELMALILI:9:118#2/r17.claim: People congratulated Ka‘b and he borrowed clothes to go to the Prophet; among the Emigrants only Ṭalḥa stood, hurried to greet and congratulate him, a kindness Ka‘b remembered.

ELMALILI:9:118#2/r18.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:9:118#2/r18.speaker: Ka‘b b. Mâlik
ELMALILI:9:118#2/r18.claim: The Prophet’s face shone with joy; he told Ka‘b that this was the best day since his birth and that the good news came from God.

ELMALILI:9:118#2/r19.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:9:118#2/r19.speaker: Ka‘b b. Mâlik
ELMALILI:9:118#2/r19.claim: Ka‘b offered to give all his wealth in charity as repentance, but the Prophet advised him to keep part; he retained his share at Khaybar.

ELMALILI:9:118#2/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:9:118#2/r2.speaker: Ka‘b b. Mâlik
ELMALILI:9:118#2/r2.claim: He was unusually capable and well supplied for Tabūk, having two riding camels available, yet still failed to prepare in time.

ELMALILI:9:118#2/r20.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:9:118#2/r20.speaker: Ka‘b b. Mâlik
ELMALILI:9:118#2/r20.claim: Ka‘b pledged to speak only truth for the rest of his life and said that, after Islam, no blessing surpassed being truthful rather than perishing through lies; he hoped God would protect him from lying.

ELMALILI:9:118#2/r21.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:9:118#2/r21.speaker: Ka‘b b. Mâlik
ELMALILI:9:118#2/r21.claim: Ka‘b says God’s revelation condemned the oath-taking liars and that he and his two companions were left waiting because their cases were deferred, not because they had simply failed to join the expedition.

ELMALILI:9:118#2/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:9:118#2/r3.speaker: Ka‘b b. Mâlik
ELMALILI:9:118#2/r3.claim: Unlike usual expeditions, the Prophet disclosed the destination because Tabūk was hot, distant, desert terrain, and faced a large enemy; the numerous Muslims were not all registered, so an absence might go unnoticed.

ELMALILI:9:118#2/r4.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:9:118#2/r4.speaker: Ka‘b b. Mâlik
ELMALILI:9:118#2/r4.claim: The expedition began during the season of ripe fruit and pleasant shade; Ka‘b repeatedly delayed preparations, assuming he could make them later.

ELMALILI:9:118#2/r5.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:9:118#2/r5.speaker: Ka‘b b. Mâlik
ELMALILI:9:118#2/r5.claim: After the army departed, Ka‘b kept trying to prepare but did nothing, then regretted not mounting a camel to catch up; in Medina he encountered only hypocrites or people with excuses.

ELMALILI:9:118#2/r6.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:9:118#2/r6.speaker: Ka‘b b. Mâlik
ELMALILI:9:118#2/r6.claim: At Tabūk the Prophet asked what Ka‘b had done; a man of Banū Salima blamed his clothes and appearance, while Mu‘ādh b. Jabal defended him as known only for good, and the Prophet remained silent.

ELMALILI:9:118#2/r7.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:9:118#2/r7.speaker: Ka‘b b. Mâlik
ELMALILI:9:118#2/r7.claim: On the return, Ka‘b considered lying and sought advice, but when the Prophet arrived he abandoned false excuses and resolved to tell the truth.

ELMALILI:9:118#2/r8.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:9:118#2/r8.speaker: Ka‘b b. Mâlik
ELMALILI:9:118#2/r8.claim: More than eighty others offered excuses and swore oaths; the Prophet accepted their outward declarations, left their inward state to God, and prayed for their forgiveness. Ka‘b admitted he had no excuse.

ELMALILI:9:118#2/r9.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:9:118#2/r9.speaker: Ka‘b b. Mâlik
ELMALILI:9:118#2/r9.claim: Ka‘b reasoned that a lie might please the Prophet briefly but would anger God against him, whereas truthful admission could leave him hoping for God’s forgiveness.

ELMALILI:9:118#3/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:9:118#3/r1.speaker: Ulemâ
ELMALILI:9:118#3/r1.claim: The scholars call repentance like that of Ka‘b and his companions sincere repentance: regret should make the world feel constricted and the self press painfully, leaving one to turn to God alone with sincerity.

ELMALILI:9:118/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:9:118/r1.speaker: author
ELMALILI:9:118/r1.claim: The three left behind are Ka‘b b. Mālik, Hilāl b. Umayya, and Murāra b. al-Rabī‘, whose cases were deferred, unlike those whose confession and repentance were accepted immediately; Ka‘b had pledged at al-‘Aqaba and his companions fought at Badr.

ELMALILI:9:118/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:9:118/r2.speaker: author
ELMALILI:9:118/r2.claim: The earth felt constricted because people would not look at or deal with them, and they could find nowhere to stay with reassurance.

ELMALILI:9:118/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:9:118/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:9:118/r3.claim: Their own consciences also tormented them: they were deeply distressed and could find neither peace nor consolation; their hearts became a prison.

ELMALILI:9:118/r4.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:9:118/r4.speaker: author
ELMALILI:9:118/r4.claim: They understood through experience that only turning to God in repentance and seeking forgiveness could save them from His anger, so they abandoned other hopes and trusted wholly in Him.

ELMALILI:9:118/r5.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:9:118/r5.speaker: author
ELMALILI:9:118/r5.claim: The phrase that God turned to them so they might repent can mean that He revealed a verse confirming acceptance, or that He again regarded them with mercy, acceptance, and enabling so they would remain firm in repentance.

ELMALILI:9:118/r6.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:9:118/r6.speaker: author
ELMALILI:9:118/r6.claim: God alone is the abundant acceptor of repentance and the possessor of limitless mercy; no sin is too numerous or great for His gracious acceptance of repentance.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v11p51#3/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v11p51#3/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v11p51#3/r1.claim: The phrase about the three coordinates with the Prophet in 9:117, repeating the preposition because of distance; these are a distinct group from other stragglers.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v11p51#3/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v11p51#3/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v11p51#3/r2.claim: The three are known as Ka'b ibn Malik, Murara ibn al-Rabi, and Hilal ibn Umayya, all Ansar who stayed behind from Tabuk without excuse, admitted guilt, were shunned and separated from their wives, then pardoned after fifty nights.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v11p51#3/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v11p51#3/r3.speaker: كعب بن مالك
IBNASHUR-FULL:v11p51#3/r3.claim: Ka'b's long account of the episode is recorded in both Sahih collections and cited by al-Baghawi.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v11p51#3/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v11p51#3/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v11p51#3/r4.claim: خلفوا is the passive of a normally intransitive verb for remaining behind; it can be construed as their leaving themselves behind or, metaphorically, having their case deferred.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v11p51#3/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v11p51#3/r5.speaker: كعب بن مالك
IBNASHUR-FULL:v11p51#3/r5.claim: Ka'b explains that they were not left behind from the expedition; rather, the Prophet deferred their cases unlike those whose excuses he accepted.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v11p52/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v11p52/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v11p52/r1.claim: They did not leave themselves behind; someone left them waiting without judgment, with the implied agent being either the Prophet or God.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v11p52/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v11p52/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v11p52/r2.claim: Attaching the ruling to the three as persons means it applies to a relevant state inferred from context, as in the prohibition of carrion at 5:3.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v11p52/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v11p52/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v11p52/r3.claim: The earth seeming cramped is a metaphor for grief and the Muslims' estrangement from them.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v11p52/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v11p52/r4.speaker: الطرماح
IBNASHUR-FULL:v11p52/r4.claim: Al-Tirimmakh's verse depicts the earth filling around someone until it appears narrow in his eyes.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v11p52/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v11p52/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v11p52/r5.claim: The deferred-case interpretation fits the endpoint of their distress; merely lagging behind on the expedition would have no endpoint.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v11p53/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v11p53/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v11p53/r1.claim: The circumstantial phrase بما رحبت uses باء for accompaniment and ما as a verbal noun: the earth is wide as commonly known.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v11p53/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v11p53/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v11p53/r2.claim: The constriction of their selves metaphorically expresses grief, as Arabic idiom says the sad person's chest narrows and the happy person's expands.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v11p53/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v11p53/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v11p53/r3.claim: ظن means certainty here: they knew only God could grant their pardon, turned to Him alone, and awaited His forgiveness, as in 2:46 and 7:66.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v11p53/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v11p53/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v11p53/r4.claim: God's later acceptance follows their distress; ثم marks temporal delay, not rank, and the clause supplies the answer to إذا.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v11p53/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v11p53/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v11p53/r5.claim: The purpose ليتوبوا means that they would persist in repentance and cease wrongdoing, not that they would sin so as to repent.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v11p53/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v11p53/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v11p53/r6.claim: The closing description of God as the Oft-Returning and Merciful is a concluding expression of favor.

TABATABAI:9:111-123#2/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:9:111-123#2/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:9:111-123#2/r2.claim: Takhalluf means leaving something behind; rahb means spaciousness, so ‘the earth despite its breadth’ describes their distress even in a wide world.

TABATABAI:9:111-123#2/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:9:111-123#2/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:9:111-123#2/r3.claim: The verses address distinct groups and kinds of repentance—some in the first group had not sinned, while the three laggards had—but the syntax joins them into one statement revealed together.

TABATABAI:9:111-123#2/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:9:111-123#2/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:9:111-123#2/r4.claim: The chief purpose is to describe God’s pardon of the three laggards; mention of the Prophet, Emigrants, and Helpers reassures them by placing all groups on equal terms after pardon.

TABATABAI:9:111-123#2/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:9:111-123#2/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:9:111-123#2/r5.claim: The repeated repentance follows an overview-then-detail structure: God’s repentance is first stated for everyone, then specified for each group and finally for the three so that they may repent.

TABATABAI:9:111-123#3/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:9:111-123#3/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:9:111-123#3/r4.claim: The three were socially shunned even by their families, grieved continuously, and became certain that repentance was their only refuge; God then guided them to repent and forgave them.

TABATABAI:9:111-123#4/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:9:111-123#4/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:9:111-123#4/r3.claim: Because God’s tawba precedes their repentance, it means the first tawba, guidance that enables them to repent.

TABATABAI:9:111-123#4/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:9:111-123#4/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:9:111-123#4/r4.claim: Calling God compassionate and merciful supports the enabling-guidance reading, since the verse names no attribute explicitly denoting acceptance.

TABATABAI:9:111-123#4/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:9:111-123#4/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:9:111-123#4/r5.claim: The pronoun in “so that they repent” refers to the three left behind; they repent after God guides them, and God then accepts and forgives.

TABATABAI:9:111-123#4/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:9:111-123#4/r6.speaker: author
TABATABAI:9:111-123#4/r6.claim: Although the wording alone does not state acceptance, the story is established by transmission and the verse’s broad tawba language and final names make rejection of their repentance impossible; 4:17 confirms acceptance.

TABATABAI:9:111-123#5/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:9:111-123#5/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:9:111-123#5/r1.claim: The claim that “so that they repent” means God merely made repentance easy is a weak interpretation.

TABATABAI:9:111-123#5/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:9:111-123#5/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:9:111-123#5/r2.claim: He rejects interpreting their repentance as a return to their pre-sin condition.

TABATABAI:9:111-123#5/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:9:111-123#5/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:9:111-123#5/r3.claim: He also rejects taking the pronoun as referring to all believers, who would repent after hearing that God accepts repentance.

TABATABAI:9:111-123#5/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:9:111-123#5/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:9:111-123#5/r4.claim: In this context, zann conveys certainty by contextual implication, not by the word’s lexical meaning.

ASAD-NOTES:9:117#n155/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:9:117#n155/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:9:117#n155/r1.claim: Although the phrase can mean 'those left behind,' Asad renders alladhina khullifu as those who became morally altered or corrupt, based on its figurative Arabic sense and support from major philologists including al-Asma'i.

ASAD-NOTES:9:117#n155/r2.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:9:117#n155/r2.speaker: classical commentators
ASAD-NOTES:9:117#n155/r2.claim: Classical commentators identify the three as Ka'b ibn Malik, Mararah ibn al-Rabi', and Hilal ibn Umayyah, who abstained from Tabuk and were ostracized until revelation; Asad accepts their historical failure but rejects restricting the verse to them.

ASAD-NOTES:9:117#n155/r3.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:9:117#n155/r3.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:9:117#n155/r3.claim: Asad takes 'the three' to mean three groups: those excused after equivocal reasons, those who stayed without permission and later repented, and those whose cases were deferred and who repented after Tabuk.

ASAD-NOTES:9:117#n156/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:9:117#n156/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:9:117#n156/r1.claim: Beyond the historical case, the verse applies to believers who stray temporarily, recognize their corruption—spontaneously or after rebuke—and sincerely repent.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:9:118/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:9:118/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:9:118/r1.claim: The three who regretted missing Tabuk but did not promptly excuse themselves or repent were Ka‘b b. Malik, Hilal b. Umayya, and Murara b. Rabi‘; after the Prophet’s return they were shunned for about fifty days until their sincere repentance was accepted.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:9:118/r2.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:9:118/r2.speaker: some interpreters
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:9:118/r2.claim: Some translate the people ‘left behind’ as those who stayed behind from the Tabuk campaign.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:9:118/r3.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:9:118/r3.speaker: most commentators
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:9:118/r3.claim: Most commentators, linking this verse to 9:106 and supported by reports from the Companions involved, prefer ‘those whose pardon was deferred.’

STUDYQURAN:9:118/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:9:118/r1.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:9:118/r1.claim: The verse concerns three men who stayed behind and made no excuses before the Prophet's departure for Tabūk or after his return.

STUDYQURAN:9:118/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:9:118/r2.speaker: Q, R
STUDYQURAN:9:118/r2.claim: Some interpret being left behind as waiting for God's judgment, rather than being physically left behind from the Tabūk expedition.

STUDYQURAN:9:118/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:9:118/r3.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:9:118/r3.claim: The sources relate that Kaʿb ibn Mālik repeatedly delayed preparations through indecision and was left in Madinah with the other two when the army departed.

STUDYQURAN:9:118/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:9:118/r4.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:9:118/r4.claim: Kaʿb refused to invent an excuse, admitted he had none, and said he had never been better prepared for battle; he had joined many earlier battles with the Prophet.

STUDYQURAN:9:118/r5.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:9:118/r5.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:9:118/r5.claim: The Prophet told Kaʿb and the other two to await God's decision, and the community was ordered to shun them.

STUDYQURAN:9:118/r6.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:9:118/r6.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:9:118/r6.claim: During the fifty-day silence Kaʿb continued walking in the markets and praying in mosques, while the other two stayed home.

STUDYQURAN:9:118/r7.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:9:118/r7.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:9:118/r7.claim: The earth closing in despite its breadth evokes constriction and loneliness, echoing the image in 9:25.

STUDYQURAN:9:intro/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:9:intro/r2.speaker: Āl
STUDYQURAN:9:intro/r2.claim: Āl connects the name al-Tawbah to God's relenting toward the Prophet and believers in 9:117–118; the same verb is rendered repent or relent with different following prepositions.

STUDYQURAN:9:intro/r6.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:9:intro/r6.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:9:intro/r6.claim: The sūrah treats loyalty and allegiance through nomadic Arabs, hypocrites' rival mosque, and Muslims wavering in their commitment to follow the Prophet into battle.
